title: Love in separation
hookLine: a week of goodbyes, and a life story that ends not in triumph but in longing
carry: vipralambha: missing krishna is still love
tomorrow: a book built like an ocean. why waves, not chapters?

cards: Missing someone can start before they've even gone: the last dinner, the half-packed suitcase, a song that suddenly hurts. The Chaitanya Charitamrita ends inside that feeling. Night in Puri, near the sea.

Chaitanya isn't dancing in the street now. He's in a small room with close companions, and he can't sleep, longing for Krishna the way Radha longs when Krishna is away. A life story might be expected to end in triumph.

teach.h: A MOMENT FEELS LIKE AN AGE.
teach.b: To get through the night, he recites verses kept under his name as the Shikshashtakam, and explains them one by one.

Near the end comes this, in paraphrase: a moment feels like an age; my eyes pour tears like rain; without Govinda, the whole world feels empty. Then the last verse. Let him hold me close, or trample me underfoot.
Let him break my heart by staying out of sight. He's free to do as he likes.

teach.h: HE ALONE IS THE LORD OF MY LIFE.
teach.b: He alone is the lord of my life, and no one else. Here's why the book can end there. It began with Krishna coming as Chaitanya to taste Radha's love.

It ends with Chaitanya tasting the hardest part of it, the missing. And the Charitamrita doesn't treat that longing as love failing. It treats the longing as love itself, still holding on when nothing comes back.
Gaudiya teachers call it vipralambha, love in separation.

teach.h: THE MISSING IS LOVE, HOLDING ON.
teach.b: For anyone in a week of goodbyes, it offers something plain: missing someone isn't a problem to fix. It can be the shape love takes while they're away.
Then the author signs off as he has all along, at the feet of his teachers, Rupa and Raghunatha.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnavas recite and sing the Shikshashtakam, the verses kept under Chaitanya's name, including its last verses on longing for Krishna.

o: a sorrow to be cured by more practice
devotion that keeps loving in the missing
a feeling that ends once God is found

games.q: the last chapter — tap the pairs.
p: night in Puri, longing for Krishna

s: the Charitamrita ends with Chaitanya's triumph in the streets
it ends at night in Puri, in longing, with his last verses.
in the last verse, whatever he does, he alone is the lord of my life
hold me close or trample me, he's still the lord of my life.
in this book, longing is a sign that love has failed
the book treats the longing as love itself, still holding on.

games.q: a friend's dad is working overseas for months. she says missing him this much means she isn't coping. what does the Charitamrita's ending suggest?
o: missing can be the shape love takes while someone's away.
keep busy until the feeling finally stops.
missing him this much means the bond is weakening.
games.why: the book ends on Chaitanya's longing and treats it as love still holding on. if missing someone ever turns into not coping at all, that's worth telling a trusted adult.

practice: Bring to mind someone you miss, near or far. If you like, write them a short message, just a line, and decide later whether to send it. Then breathe slowly beside the missing, without trying to fix it.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti, at the book's end: a love that keeps holding on in the dark, whatever comes back.

orig.note: Sanskrit vipralambha, love in separation; the longing in which the Charitamrita ends.

carryVoice: Carry this: vipralambha, missing Krishna is still love. The Chaitanya Charitamrita closes here.

sources.ref: Chaitanya Charitamrita, Antya-lila 20 (Chaitanya in Puri at night with close companions, in longing for Krishna; reciting and explaining the Shikshashtakam; verse 7: a moment like an age, tears like rain, the world empty without Govinda; verse 8: embrace or trample me, he alone is the lord of my life; the author's closing at the feet of Rupa and Raghunatha)
